inbox.originalContent: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.

history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx), proposed by Harvard University, aimed to explore the behavior of aerosol particles in the stratosphere. Led by Frank Keutsch and his team, the initiative was publicly discussed, including at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. Importantly, SCoPEx was not intended as a deployment of solar geoengineering but rather as a scientific study to enhance computer models assessing the risks and benefits of solar radiation management. The experiment was to utilize a balloon gondola at approximately 20 km altitude, releasing a very small quantity of materials, typically calcium carbonate, into a controlled area to measure aerosol microphysics and chemistry. A planned platform test in Sweden focused solely on hardware evaluation and was suspended pending societal engagement, with no particles released. In March 2024, Harvard announced the discontinuation of SCoPEx, with plans to repurpose the platform for unrelated stratospheric research, underscoring the importance of focusing on emissions reductions and maintaining net-zero commitments.
